summary:
Your field has shifted. Has your plan?

Terrasight is an AI assistant for farmers and agronomists. It turns 45 years of NASA POWER weather, MODIS satellite greenness and USDA and ESA Copernicus open data into two things a farm can act on: a daily, explained recommendation for every field, and a five-season crop rotation plan (2026–2030).

It answers the challenge directly. For a real field in Kansas it shows how the climate has shifted (first autumn frost 9 days later, a longer frost-free season), then tests each rotation on 150 weather runs and 10 price scenarios; the recommended one earns $32 per acre a year more than today's.

Why it matters: farmers cannot adapt to a change they cannot see or trust. Every number the assistant says is checked against the models, and a dedicated page shows where the model was wrong: 4 of the last 10 seasons, shown, not hidden.
details:
The problem

Farmers keep hearing that the climate is changing. Nobody tells them what changed on their field, or what to plant next season because of it. Terrasight does.

What it does

Terrasight is an AI assistant for farmers and agronomists. Draw a field on a satellite map, and 45 years of NASA weather, satellite greenness, soil and crop history for that exact place go to work.

Every morning it tells you what to do first, and why: pest and disease risk, frost, irrigation, and the best days this week for spraying, sowing and harvest.

It shows how your climate has shifted. On North quarter, a dryland field in Finney County, Kansas, NASA POWER data since 1981 show the first autumn frost coming 9 days later, a frost-free period 12.8 days longer and 169 more growing degree days. Where there is no clear trend, it says so.

It plans five seasons ahead (2026–2030). Each rotation is tested on 150 weather runs and 10 price scenarios. For this field the recommended rotation (winter wheat, sorghum, sunflower, fallow) earns $32 per acre a year more than today's. The agronomist proposes; the farm owner approves in one tap.

It answers your questions. Ask anything about a field in plain language. The language model writes the words only; every number comes from our models and is checked before you see it.

How it is creative: it shows where it was wrong

Most decision tools show their best numbers. Terrasight has a page called "How far can you trust this". It reruns the model over past seasons with the weather that really happened and compares it with official USDA yields and MODIS satellite greenness: r = 0.71 and r = 0.82 over 10 years. Then it lists the years it missed (2012, 2014, 2022, 2023) and why. In the 2022 drought the model said −11%; the official record was −46%. We show that, because an assistant that admits its limits is one a farmer can trust.and why. In the 2022 drought the model said −11%; the official record was −46%. We show that, because an assistant that admits its limits is one a farmer can trust.

Benefits and intended impact

- A change you can see. Climate shift stops being a headline and becomes a few plain sentences about your own field.

- A plan you can defend. Every option is tested against bad years and price swings, not one average season.

- Evidence with every answer. Reliability, data level and sources sit next to each recommendation.

- Works beyond the US. Full data in the US, basic data in the EU, estimates worldwide, including Ukraine. English and Ukrainian.

Our goal: make adapting a farm to a shifted climate a routine, checkable decision instead of a guess.

What we considered

- Safety: risk, never a diagnosis; no pesticide products or doses.

- AI on a short leash: the language model never produces a number.

- Honest economics: gross margin only; decisions rest on the difference from the current rotation.

- Honest limits: heat, frost and harvest losses are not modelled yet; on irrigated fields the model cannot be checked against yields, and the app says so; the GPM IMERG rainfall check is written but not yet verified, so no result uses it.

Tools and languages

TypeScript throughout: Next.js and React, NestJS, PostgreSQL with PostGIS, Prisma, RabbitMQ, Redis, MapLibre GL, Docker; Jest, Vitest, Playwright and Cypress for tests. The models are our own implementations of FAO-56 and FAO-33 water balance, SCS-CN runoff, ICBM soil carbon and a Monte Carlo simulator. Google Gemini API for wording and for the demo narration voices.

The company and people shown (Prairie Field Co., Olena Kovalenko, Marko Shevchenko) are a fictional persona. The fields and all data are real.
